notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, as the county reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
Payments to other governments ($920,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts contributions from businesses, PACs and unions to county executive, council, commission, sheriff and other county office candidates, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023 (92 receipts). Individuals, candidates' own money, parties and unidentified small gifts are not counted. Candidates who raise little can use mini-reporting and itemize nothing, so some money may be missing.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: License-plate readers
redFlags.detail: The Kitsap County Sheriff's Office has used automated license plate readers since at least 2013.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS007482, citing Seattle Times

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Kitsap County Sheriff's Office operates one DJI Mavic drone as of 2018, according to data compiled by the Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS003456, citing Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College

Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. Residents also pay Kitsap County.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
Debt service leaves out $574,000 of principal repaid with new borrowing the city did not spend on capital that year, most likely refinancing or a rolled-over note.
Payments to other governments ($225,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts contributions from businesses, PACs and unions to candidates for mayor and city or town council, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023 (13 receipts). Individuals, candidates' own money, parties and unidentified small gifts are not counted. Candidates who raise little can use mini-reporting and itemize nothing, so some money may be missing.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 1 license-plate camera is mapped inside City of Port Orchard's borders in OpenStreetMap (1 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.
